items.title: Paramount files new legal statement saying states' antitrust suit misses the whole point of the merger
items.author: William Hughes

items.text:
Although they’re technically headed—due to a legally mandated step set forward by a judge—to the settlement negotiation table next month, Paramount and the coalition of state attorneys general currently trying to stand as the last roadblock in the company’s efforts to buy Warner Bros. moved past the point of civil conversation at least one “We’ll take the whole damn company out of Hollywood if you’re not careful” threat ago. As such, it’s not surprising that Paramount’s legal filings in the slowly brewing court case between the two are getting pretty belligerent, as the David Ellison-owned media company filed a new legal document on Friday that attempted a point-by-point dismantling of the states’ case. “Day by day,” the company’s lawyers write, “The weak case against this Merger gets even weaker.”


The gist of the argument, which was filed as a response to the AGs’ initial complaint, is one we’ve seen from Paramount before, back when it was getting bogged down in arguments about whether Curry Barker’s indie horror hit Obsession counts as a “blockbuster”: That the states’ case against the merger is built off of an older understanding of Hollywood that sees major studios like Paramount and Warner Bros. as main, direct rivals for each other—which ignores, they argue, the reality of tech-derived companies like Netflix, Apple, and Amazon breaking into the market over the course of the 21st century. In what, to the best of our knowledge, is the only legal filing between a large Hollywood studios and 12 American states to acknowledge the existence of that upcoming Netflix theatrical movie where Taika Waititi plays an ex-con Willy Wonka, the response argues that the streamers are already stomping all over the theatrical market, and that the only way for old Hollywood (as represented by David Ellison, a guy who’s owned a major studio for all of two years because his tech billionaire dad gave him some pocket change) to fight back is to merge into a cinematic kaiju of its own. (The Godzilla metaphor is our own, sadly, and not part of the legal filing.)


There are other aspects to the response, with Paramount making the requisite attacks on the states’ ability to litigate an antitrust issue that’s already been cheerfully cleared by Ellison’s buddies in the Department Of Justice. (With the paragraph-by-paragraph addressing of each of the original complaint’s points including such lawyers-are-certainly-human-beings-type language as “Defendants admit that the State of Oregon is a state of the United States.”) Among other things, the filing points to the fact that all three of America’s major theater chains have stated that they want the merger, apparently convinced of Ellison’s claims that ParaBros. (or whatever they end up calling this new city-stomping behemoth) will keep big movies rolling out at a steady pace. (The assertion that Cinema United, the trade organization representing the chains, is calling for a settlement in the case does blithely paper over the fact that the group has not actually gone so far as to endorse the plan, though.)


There will, of course, be more of these backs-and-forths as the negotiations approach and then, it seems very probable, recede. (Both sides are reportedly pretty intransigent in their belief in the merits of their arguments; also, given the politicized overtones of all this, we’d be shocked if any of these AGs blinked before the elections in November.) The most interesting aspect of the whole thing, meanwhile, might come down to a point not articulated in Paramount’s new filing at all: Whether (per Variety) Paramount will get its demand that the states pony up a bond covering the costs of delaying the merger, estimated at nearly $2 billion thanks to the “ticking fee” Paramount agreed to give Warner Bros. if the sale got delayed. Even split across 12 states, that’s a lot of cash, with Paramount clearly attempting to extract some real blood in exchange for the AGs attempts to get in the way of its big kaiju dreams.

items.text:
Tom Cruise’s Epic Historical Masterpiece Is Officially Storming the Streaming Charts Again

Image via Roger Wong/INSTARimages.com

Published Sep 13, 2026, 5:40 AM EDT

In over three years at Collider, senior author Jake has now penned over 3000 articles covering a wide range of TV and film for the resources, lists, utilities, news, and interview teams. Alongside interviewing stars such as Selin Hizli, Rose Ayling-Ellis, Harlan Coben, and Chelsea Peretti, Jake was lucky enough to visit the set of Aardman and Netflix's Wallace and Gromit: A Vengeance Most Fowl in 2024, getting the chance to chat with four-time Academy Award winner Nick Park and Merlin Crossingham. Jake has also worked for other publications, including Agents of Fandom. You can also hear Jake every week as the resident film and TV journalist on Track Radio.

The historical epic is a staple of cinema, and it's currently proving to be one of the most popular genres. The 21st century's headline filmmaker Christopher Nolan delivered the most ambitious of its kind in recent memory with his adaptation of Homer's ancient Greek epic The Odyssey, which debuted this summer. Dubbed an "unrivaled cinematic spectacle" in Joe Schmidt's review for Collider, The Odyssey is likely to sweep up at the 2027 Academy Awards, and might even break the nominations record set by Ryan Coogler's Sinners this year.

Having made over $1.6 billion at the box office and still sailing towards new milestones, The Odyssey is far and away the biggest success in Nolan's filmography, and is also the highest-grossing historical epic of all time. Part of its success can be attributed to its star-studded ensemble, led by Matt Damon as the King of Ithaca, and including Lupita Nyong’o, Charlize Theron, Anne Hathaway, Tom Holland, Jon Bernthal, Zendaya, and Robert Pattinson.

The historical epic genre's biggest hit of all time is encouraging fans to seek other examples on streaming. One such example is The Last Samurai, the 2003 gem set in 1878 during the Meiji period in Japan. Hollywood veteran Tom Cruise stars in the film as Civil War veteran Captain Nathan Algren, as he joins forces with director Edward Zwick before the pair would make Jack Reacher: Never Go Back. Also starring Ken Watanabe, Hiroyuki Sanada, Timothy Spall, and others, The Last Samurai is a true hidden treasure in the historical epic genre and is currently one of the ten most-streamed movies on HBO Max in the U.S.

Collider Exclusive · Action Hero Quiz
Which Action Hero Would Be
Your Perfect Partner?
Rambo · James Bond · Indiana Jones · John McClane · Ethan Hunt

Five legends. Five completely different ways of getting out alive — with style, with muscle, with charm, with luck, or with a plan so intricate it probably shouldn't work. Ten questions will reveal which action hero was built to have your back.

🎖️Rambo

🍸James Bond

🏺Indiana Jones

🔧John McClane

🎭Ethan Hunt

FIND YOUR PARTNER →

01

You're dropped into a dangerous situation with no warning. What do you need most from a partner?
The first few seconds tell you everything about who belongs beside you.

ASomeone who already has three contingency plans running and is calmly working through all of them.
BSomeone who reads the terrain instinctively and knows exactly how to use it against the enemy.
CSomeone who keeps their nerve and their sense of humour when everything is falling apart.
DSomeone who knows the history of wherever we are and what we're walking into.
ESomeone with the right contact, the right cover identity, and the right exit already arranged.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

You have to get somewhere dangerous, fast. How do you travel?
How you get there is half the mission.

AOn foot through terrain no one else would attempt — I move where vehicles can't follow.
BOn a motorcycle, a cargo plane, or anything else that gets me there before I think too hard about it.
CIn something that belongs to someone else — borrowed, stolen, or improvised under fire.
DFirst class, with a cover identity and a gadget that does something I won't explain until it's needed.
EBy whatever means are available — I've driven, flown, and once arrived by camel. The destination matters, not the method.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

You're pinned down and outnumbered. What does your ideal partner do?
This is when you find out what someone is really made of.

ADisappears into the environment, flanks them silently, and ends it before I've reloaded.
BCracks a one-liner, grabs a fire extinguisher or a chair, and improvises something that somehow works.
CProduces a gadget specifically designed for this exact scenario and uses it with infuriating precision.
DPulls out a whip, a pistol, and an archaeological insight that somehow gets us out alive.
ENeutralises the threat with maximum efficiency and minimum words — they were already three moves ahead.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

The mission is paused. You have one evening to decompress. What does your partner suggest?
Who someone is when the pressure drops is who they actually are.

AA bar with terrible lighting, cold beer, and absolutely no questions about feelings.
BThe finest restaurant in the city, a bottle of something expensive, and a conversation that is equal parts brilliant and exhausting.
CA local dig site, a museum after hours, or a long story about why that particular artefact matters to human civilisation.
DPizza. Bad TV. Falling asleep halfway through a movie neither of you were watching anyway.
EA debrief that turns into three hours of contingency planning that somehow becomes the most fun you've had all week.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

How do you prefer your partner to communicate mid-mission?
Good communication is the difference between partners and a liability.

APrecise and minimal — tell me what I need to know and nothing else. Every word has a cost.
BDeadpan and dry — keeping it light keeps me sharp, even when everything is on fire.
CEnthusiastic and slightly chaotic — but always with useful information buried somewhere in the noise.
DCalm and controlled through an earpiece, with a plan that covers every variable I haven't thought of yet.
EBarely at all — silence is a language and they speak it fluently.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

Your enemy is powerful, well-resourced, and has the upper hand. How should your partner approach them?
The approach to the enemy defines the partnership.

AInfiltrate their inner circle, learn everything, and dismantle them from inside out before they know we're there.
BStudy the historical pattern — every villain of this type has a weakness written somewhere in the past.
CGet them talking. The more they monologue, the more time I have to figure out how to beat them.
DGo through them. Directly. With as much force as the terrain allows.
EFind the one thing they haven't accounted for — there's always one thing — and make sure we're holding it.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

Things go badly wrong and you're captured. What do you trust your partner to do?
Who someone is when you need them most is the only thing that matters.

ACome in alone, quietly, and get me out before anyone knows they were there.
BHave already been working on the extraction since the moment I disappeared — the plan is already running.
CCome in loud, come in fast, and worry about the collateral damage later — I'd do the same for them.
DUse every resource, every contact, and bend every rule until I'm out — they don't leave people behind.
ECharm their way in somehow, bluff through the hard part, and still manage to look good doing it.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

What does your ideal partner bring to the table that you couldn't replace?
A great partner fills the gap you didn't know you had.

ATechnology that shouldn't exist yet and the training to use it under any conditions.
BSurvival instinct so refined it borders on supernatural — and the scars to prove it's been tested.
CKnowledge of history, language, and culture that makes them invaluable in places where force is useless.
DThe ability to walk into any room in the world and immediately become the most trusted person in it.
EStubbornness that refuses to accept a situation is hopeless — and the improvisational skill to back it up.

NEXT QUESTION →

09

Every partnership has a cost. Which of these can you live with?
No one comes without baggage. The question is whether you can carry it together.

AA partner who never fully switches off — always watching exits, always calculating threats, even at dinner.
BA partner who gets the job done brilliantly but has the emotional availability of a locked filing cabinet.
CA partner who makes everything ten times more complicated than it needs to be — but who always comes through.
DA partner who gets personally attached to every relic, ruin, and artefact we encounter, which slows everything down.
EA partner who was not built for this and knows it — but shows up anyway, every time, without being asked.

NEXT QUESTION →

10

It's the final moment. Everything is on the line. What do you need from your partner right now?
The last question is the most honest one.

AOne line. Absolutely dry. Delivered like the world isn't ending. Then we move.
BNothing said at all — just a look that means we both already know what has to happen.
CA plan I don't fully understand that somehow accounts for everything, delivered in thirty seconds flat.
DA piece of historical context that reframes the entire situation and tells us exactly what to do next.
ESomeone who steps forward instead of back — because that's who they've always been.

REVEAL MY PARTNER →

Your Partner Has Been Assigned
Your Perfect Partner Is…

Your answers have pointed to one action hero above all others. This is the person built to have your back — for better or considerably, spectacularly worse.

Rambo

Your partner doesn't talk much, doesn't need to, and will have assessed every threat in your immediate environment before you've finished your first sentence. John Rambo is not a man of plans or politics — he is a force of nature shaped by survival, loyalty, and a capacity for endurance that goes beyond anything training can produce. He will not leave you behind. He has never left anyone behind who deserved to come home. What you get with Rambo is the most capable, most quietly ferocious partner imaginable — one who has been through things that would have broken anyone else, and who chose to keep going anyway. You'll never need to ask if he has your back. You'll just know.

James Bond

Your partner will arrive perfectly dressed, perfectly briefed, and with a cover story so convincing it'll take you a moment to remember what's actually true. James Bond is the most professionally dangerous person in any room he enters — and the most disarmingly charming, which is the point. A Knight Of The Seven Kingdoms Returns In Winter 2026 With New Collector's Set

Published Sep 13, 2026, 2:00 AM EDT

Nicholas Becher is a gaming journalist with an MFA in Creative Writing from FAU. With extensive experience playing video games, he covers all forms of gaming content at Screen Rant, from breaking news to the latest fan theories. Most-played games range from Clair Obscur to Civ to Elden Ring to Halo 2 and beyond.

Earlier this year, it was confirmed that A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms officially wrapped up filming its second season, putting Dunk and Egg's highly anticipated return firmly on track for 2027. The quick turnaround comes after the Game of Thrones spinoff became one of HBO's biggest surprises of the year, earning widespread critical acclaim while proving enormously popular with viewers. Its premiere drew 6.7 million viewers in its first three days, while the Season 1 finale climbed to 9.5 million, capping off a remarkably successful debut run.

Season 2 will once again follow Peter Claffey's Ser Duncan the Tall and Dexter Sol Ansell's Egg, this time adapting George R.R. Martin's second Dunk and Egg novella, The Sworn Sword. Their next adventure trades the tournament at Ashford for a smaller but equally dangerous conflict in the Reach, where Dunk enters the service of Ser Eustace Osgrey and becomes caught in his dispute with the formidable Lady Rohanne Webber, better known as the Red Widow.

However, ahead of season 2's official launch next year, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is getting an official new release in winter 2026 (via SciFi Hobby).

In an upcoming release from Rittenhouse Archives, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is getting a full Season 1 set of Trading Cards sometime in Winter 2026. While official details are still rather sparse, based on the other Game of Thrones sets from Rittenhouse, the AKOTSK release will feature a trove of unique characters from the series that will likely be signed by the official actors themselves.

Rittenhouse has not yet revealed a checklist, box configuration, price, or exact release date beyond the Winter 2026 window, but its previous Westeros collections give a fairly good indication of what collectors could eventually see. The company's House of the Dragon Season 1 set featured a 50-card base collection alongside autograph cards, costume relics, foil versions, character galleries, artist renditions, episode posters, relationship cards, location cards, and hand-drawn sketches.

Every box contained one autograph and two relic cards, with all of the advertised autographs signed on-card by actors including Matt Smith, Emma D'Arcy, Paddy Considine, and Olivia Cooke. The upcoming House of the Dragon Season 2 release, scheduled for September 30, guarantees two autograph cards and one relic per box, with a hand-drawn sketch card appearing in every case. Its autograph lineup stretches well beyond the show's central stars to supporting performers such as Clinton Liberty, Kieran Bew, Phoebe Campbell, and Elliott Tittensor.

Recent Game of Thrones releases have included everything from wardrobe cards and numbered parallels to character-focused inserts, metal cards, episode artwork, and sketches. That makes Dunk and Egg obvious candidates for the centerpiece of the A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms collection, potentially with autograph cards from Peter Claffey and Dexter Sol Ansell.

Beyond the two stars, Season 1 offers an unusually strong supporting lineup for Rittenhouse to pull from. Daniel Ings' Lyonel Baratheon, Bertie Carvel's Baelor Breakspear, Sam Spruell's Maekar Targaryen, and Finn Bennett's Aerion Brightflame would all make sense, particularly given their importance to the Ashford tournament and the Trial of Seven. Further, Tanzyn Crawford's Tanselle, Shaun Thomas' Raymun Fossoway, and Danny Webb's Ser Arlan of Pennytree are other likely possibilities, while Henry Ashton's Daeron Targaryen and Edward Ashley's Steffon Fossoway could very well make an appearance too.

That said, no cards have been confirmed yet, but Rittenhouse's history of spotlighting both major and supporting characters makes a broad Season 1 roster likely, and it will be a timely release given A Knight of the Seven Kingdom's Season 2 will air in a matter of months after the card sets drop.

James is a gaming writer from London who has spent thousands of hours exploring titles from every genre. Though he has a particular affinity for multiplayer titles like World of Warcraft, Destiny 2 and League of Legends, he has also put thousands of hours into single-player experiences, from deep RPGs to epic PC strategies. When he's not playing or writing, he can usually be found supporting his beloved Brentford FC.

Blizzcon 2026 is now well underway, and all sorts of exciting announcements are going on around some of the developer's biggest and most successful titles. Diablo IV is very much one of those, with the hugely successful action RPG still going strong after the latest round of updates, following the Lord of Hatred expansion.

As is always the case with Blizzard's biggest celebration, there are plenty of free rewards to be had for those who count themselves as fans. With the event drawing to a close on September 13, here's everything you need to know about picking up those sweet in-game items before they go away forever.

As confirmed by Mobalytics, players can pick up Twitch Drops for Diablo IV, based on the amount of time watching participating channels streaming the game while Blizzcon is live. The full list of items and what you need to do to get them is as follows:

2 hours watch time: Serrated Skean (dagger).

4 hours watch time: Corroded Cleaver (axe).

6 hours watch time: Tintinnabulation (mace).

The fun doesn't stop there, as you can also get the exclusive Diablo Twitch badge by subscribing or gifting to a Diablo content creator. There are some additional items on over via the Blizzard store (which will be available a little beyond the end of the event), though you will actually have to pay for those if you want them for your account.

Specifically, the Diablo IV BlizzCon Bundle is available for $29.99 USD, and it comes with the Streamsnout pet, Indigo cat mount, and Escapeproof mount armor. Those items can also be secured by purchasing the BlizzCon Ultimate Collection Bundle ($49.99 USD), which also includes the Inidigo’s Light Mount Trophy and Indigo’s Master Mount Trophy. The UCB also includes items for other games from the company, including:

WoW

Rabbit'ath Flying Mount

Ensemble: Garb of the Dawnfire Phoenix transmog set

Perch of the Dawnfire Phoenix decor

Overwatch

Lich Queen Mei Legendary Skin

Frostmourne Ana Weapon Skin

Lichimari King Weapon Charm

Lich Queen Mei Spray

Diablo Immortal

Rimedarter Familiar Transmog

Seekers of Riddergrove (Violet) Portal

20 Legendary Crests

10 Telluric Pearls

Mother’s Lament 2-Star Legendary Gem

Hearthstone

Bloodmage Thalnos Signature Legendary

Blade of the Black Empire Card Back

5 Standard Card Packs

Those who are attending the convention in-person and have purchased an event pass for entry will also be entitled to claim the Ultimate Collection Bundle for free.

Season 15 is also expected to launch in the middle of this month, so it's a great time to jump back into Diablo IV if you haven't played for a while. Beyond that, we don't really know what's coming next just yet, but keep an eye out for major announcements during the panel for the game.

items.title: A24 somehow making an SCP movie without anybody from The SCP Foundation involved
items.author: William Hughes
items.summary: The SCP Foundation is one of the most fascinating collaborative projects in internet history: An effort, touched by thousands of hands over nearly two decades,
items.text:
The SCP Foundation is one of the most fascinating collaborative projects in internet history: An effort, touched by thousands of hands over nearly two decades, to create a shared horror universe based around a mysterious organization and its attempts to create “special containment protocols” for objects of anomalous, and frequently apocalyptic, power. Featuring horror, fantasy, science fiction, comedy, and an absolutely huge amount of black redacting bars, the site has been running for 16 years at this point, and has been the basis for any number of video games, podcasts, and online shorts. So while it was probably inevitable that Hollywood would eventually start sniffing around the project, it is a bit surprising to learn that A24 is moving forward with plans for an SCP film without anyone involved in the creation of The SCP Foundation being involved.


The studio’s involvement broke online on Friday, via a report from Deadline stating that A24 had come aboard a previously mentioned effort to adapt the SCP setting into the existing V/H/S/ horror franchise. The article noted that Image Nation Studios and Spooky Pictures were involved in the film’s production; what it didn’t mention, beyond a claim to “worldwide rights” to the project, was which members of the guiding group for The SCP Foundation Wiki might be involved.


None, apparently: In a statement to The A.V. Club, The SCP Foundation Wiki Licensing Team wrote that, although members of the team have attempted to reach out to the filmmakers about the project, “We have not had any communication with the filmmakers, producers, or distributors for this project, despite our best efforts, and to the best of our knowledge they have not made any efforts to contact us.” They also called Deadline‘s claim of “worldwide rights” “incorrect,” citing the terms of the Creative Commons ShareAlike license the entire Wiki is released under.


Ownership is the big, flashing question mark hanging over all of Hollywood’s recent efforts to shove online horror into a theater-shaped box. On the one end, you have projects like Zach Cregger and Brian Duffield’s recently announced Siren Head movie, where the duo are working from clearly copyrighted materials licensed from artist Trevor Henderson. On the other, there’s A24’s own Backrooms, which, while based on director Kane Parsons’ YouTube-published short films, was clearly beholden to the communal setting Parsons was inspired by. The SCP wiki sits in a unique position between those two extremes: The Licensing Team’s statement noted that, while many derivative works have been made using the SCP name, all such projects are required to also carry the CC BY-SA license that the entire archive, and the idea of SCPs themselves, exists under. Among other things, honoring that license means A24’s movie would need to be released without “DRM or other effective technological measures that would prevent it from being copied,” and, probably most crucially, “They would not be able to establish any sort of exclusivity with respect to distribution”—meaning the film would be freely available to upload to YouTube, or even commercial streaming platforms, without the studio being able to say a word.


Which doesn’t seem like something A24 would just put up with—something the Licensing Team’s statement notes is a major reason Hollywood has never bit on SCP before, despite its online popularity. (While also making it wild that the filmmakers would specifically use the group’s name, instead of trying to fudge around it.) We’ve reached out to A24 to try to get a response to the Foundation’s assertion of the terms of its license; so, for that matter, has the Licensing Team, which had the following to say in conclusion:


We’d love to sit down with A24, Spooky Pictures, and other involved parties to discuss options for how they could make and distribute a film while complying with our license. We chose to release our project under a Creative Commons license to allow fans to tell their own stories as well as adapt ours. We chose the ShareAlike license to ensure that everyone who enjoyed those fan works would have the same rights as the people who created them. We’re getting frustrated with this whole situation and are disappointed that these filmmakers seem to have no interest in engaging with the authors or curators of the material they’re adapting.

items.title: Wardogs presents a different kind of FPS power fantasy: making fat stacks as a pacifist rideshare driver
items.author: James Archer
items.summary: Because no-one entirely likes their job, I should be upfront about my issues with newly launched Early Access darling Wardogs, the mass-scale multiplayer
items.text:
Because no-one entirely likes their job, I should be upfront about my issues with newly launched Early Access darling Wardogs, the mass-scale multiplayer shooter in which I’ve just found employment. Its "Play like to you used to" tagline and Halo 3-aping trailer smell a bit of reactionary, stuck-in-the-past thinking. It’s a mass-scale multiplayer shooter, so individual heroics rarely influence match outcomes. And, like pretty much everyone else who sucked down both those problems and tried playing on launch night regardless, I spent far too long attempting to communicate with server architecture that clearly had the resilience of overmilked cornflakes.

And yet, the fifty minutes I did spend in a functioning match felt like some of the most pleasant and productive time I’ve had in a competitive FPS for ages. The secret: ignore all first person shooting entirely, and begin a lucrative career as an Uber driver for commuting mercs.

In a stark break from reality, Wardogs’ gig economy can be very profitable indeed. Almost every positive action earns you cash, from the obvious hardpoint captures and squadmate revives to the humble delivery of people and bandages to the frontlines. And, since team spawns are literal miles from the central battlezones, logistical roles are not merely cash-incentivised, but essential.

In an accurate reflection of reality, you begin with little, must buy all vehicles and equipment yourself, and are on the hook if they’re lost while on duty. But the creation of genuine rear-detachment roles means Wardogs solves problems I have with both big shooters, and the extraction subgenre it also borrows from: by constantly ferrying teammates, I can have an individual yet materially important impact on the match, and by never intentionally joining a gunfight, I need never worry about loot loss anxiety. It was the perfect career move.

Buoyed by first-day enthusiasm, once I finally loaded into a game I bought a car, directed it dutifully towards the crowd of pedestrian soldiers, and immediately caused a helicopter crash. My pull-up-to-the-kerb manoeuvre had unwittingly put me in the landing path of a descending attack chopper – a major fault in the standard United Kingdom driving test – forcing the delicate warbird to flip over my roof and explode. Its occupants, miraculously unhurt but quite cross, shot me a damning glance as they strode off to buy another one.

The rest of my inaugural fare, a full house of one real-life friend and two silent randomers, went mercifully smoother. Despite the slippery handling of my entry-level SUV, it was a comfortable, peaceful drive towards the hot zone, which itself offered ample parking space for my passengers to hop out. The prizes came instantly: $1,000 for a "tactical deployment", plus $500 for each of my unharmed passengers, plus a $15 tip from a particularly satisfied rider. $2,515 for a few kilometres of relaxed cruising? The hell am I doing as a deputy ed?

The private hire lifestyle took hold. For multiple runs, I’d steer back to base, wait next to other transit vehicles (sometimes sharing an “A’ight, mate” with the heli pilot next to me), load up on balaclava men, and deliver them vaguely near the sound of gunfire, my balance swelling with each trip. Half an hour in, I’d accumulated slightly higher earnings than my IRL friend, who’d been running around murdering people and getting shot himself. Sounds painful. Sounds like participating directly in the horrors of war, mankind’s most terrible creation, and a blight on the Earth that continues to destroy families and erase cultures every day. Sounds like he’s not even getting paid that much to do it anyway, the rube.

Meanwhile, my hands were clean, not counting all the filthy lucre that was crossing it. Granted, my usefulness was starting and ending with the thunk of automobile doors – sometimes I’d watch my disembarked comrades perish just moments after paying their fare, a tragically premature "Passenger survived, +$500" lingering onscreen as their heaped form shrunk in my rearview. It turned out those heli pilots were not my mates at all, but were conspiring to steal my business, adopting the unfair and likely illegal practice of having faster vehicles than me. items.title: Stylised XCOM-like tactics game Ex Sanguis straps Othercide's obsession with timelines to a leaner roguelike campaign
items.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
items.summary: The nasal greenhorn strategy gamer understands "strategy" to be about mastery of space by means of clanging offensives, shining shieldwalls, and brute
items.text:
The nasal greenhorn strategy gamer understands "strategy" to be about mastery of space by means of clanging offensives, shining shieldwalls, and brute attrition, but the true Napoleon of Drag-Select knows that strategy is always, primarily, the mastery of time. I don't think Napoleon would have approved of Ex Sanguis. He would not have liked all the willowy clone women made out of congealed blood and pincers. He would have suspected them of being divorcees and Babouvists. But perhaps he would have appreciated the game's fixation with seizing the initiative.

As with Lightbulb's previous grid-based tactics RPG Othercide, Ex Sanguis has you going up against dozens of vaguely eschatological bladespawn with just the three austere and menacing bladegirls. There are generally a half-dozen foes to start with, and reinforcements soon hatch from gross eggsacs around the map. You can't simply overwhelm your opponents, then. Instead, you must pre-empt and interrupt them, anticipating their advance and dancing your best moves in first on the game's fluctuating timeline.

Some abilities are performed instantly, while others trigger after a delay. However initially inconvenient, the delays soon become an asset, as you learn to aim your artillery strikes where you know your enemies will be, a few score ticks from now. Other abilities trigger when an opponent acts, cutting them off. Or when a friendly deals some damage, adding a follow-up attack. A key question is whether to exhaust your regular action points and dip into your Burst bar, which lets you sneak in some extra licks at the cost of wildly postponing the character's next turn.

Watch on YouTube

And then there's repositioning: you get shoves, gravity pulses, and driving kicks that punt opponents around. This allows you to knock delayed enemy attacks off target, perhaps slamming the noxious seraphim into a boulder, or nudging them into the path of the AOE move you've just queued up with the previous character. As you preview these gambits, the character portraits and action indicators shuffle to and fro on the timeline. On higher difficulties, it's vitally important to avoid a scenario where the whole opposing force can take a turn, one after the other.

When I played Othercide, I didn't quite clock how much Lightbulb's approach has in common with Into The Breach. The resemblance feels a bit more prominent in Ex Sanguis. There's no fixed match countdown, true, but you're encouraged to finish fast: the angelbeasts are only going to get more numerous, and you generally aren't required to slaughter all of them - just a surgeon's handful of VIPs or a single enemy map fixture, sulking to the rear.

It's a messier experience than you'll find in Subset's game, however. The environments are full of blood blisters that blow up when struck, launching nearby characters a few squares. On more crowded maps, a single volatile pustule often triggers a prolonged cascade. The AI in the early access build seems overfond of setting the blisters off, in addition to controlling terrain. Some times, it's hellbent on swarming you; at others, it tries to lock down big portions of the map by preparing a delayed AOE move, wherever it finds itself.

The greater emphasis on terrain damage is one thing that distinguishes the early access version of Ex Sanguis from what I remember of Othercide. The other, more obvious point of departure is that Ex Sanguis has a trimmer roguelike structure, with more focussed progression.

On which note, here's my best effort at explaining the story: some kind of pesky vampire moon has leeched away the world's vital fluids and memories, reducing all of Creation to an ivory placeholder. You are the Mater, a goddess replete with the simmering intensity of Derek Zoolander. She can spawn duplicates of herself to fight the moon's minions. So far, it's very much the previous game's gothic mommy monster mash on fast-forward – all pout and glare and cod Latin metaphors, without much coherence but with a lot of enjoyable attitude.

It feels faster partly because there's less going on outside battle. Each run kicks you off with three warriors, allowing you to pick their classes – the initial options are broadly Swordlady, Gunlass and Time Wizardress - and starting abilities. You then trek across a cratered world map, fighting battles (with unlockable higher difficulties) and accumulating Corrupted Blood for campaign progression. Every battle you win nets you a choice of three further abilities or stat boosts per character.

Yes, we are operating in the realm of Vampire Survivors, just a teeny bit. As in the previous game and many other roguelikes, abilities form complementary sets, which are fun to unearth: for example, Swordlady can inflict bleed with one kind of melee attack, then slurp up the debuff to restore her own health. Eventually, you swill down enough Corrupted Blood from victories to access a bossfight, which functions as a chapter break. It's wise, of course, to pootle around a bit first, levelling up your murderdames and spending a bit of your Corrupted Blood on smaller lore discoveries that come with bonus abilities. When a run is over, whether due to beating a boss or defeat, you'll spend various flavours of ethereal substance on meta-unlocks that give you more things to unlock within runs.

I'm mixed on the new campaign format. I do miss the grottier, denser storytelling of the previous game, which grounded its stark monochrome abstractions in a narrative of obscure medieval abuses: it was like a neo-noir penny dreadful. I also took ghoulish pleasure in the ability to melt down your clone-daughters into primordial soup, treating the weaker ones as health packs for their more accomplished sisters, rather than just levelling everybody up. It's possible there are similarly revolting ideas at play later in Ex Sanguis.

Beyond that, I do wonder how much the new game's battle system and ability design really improves on Othercide's. I haven't yet discovered a blend of reaction and delayed abilities that really captivates me, in terms of how it lets me mess with the timeline and disrupt the horde.

Still, it's early days – I've only played three hours, and Ex Sanguis will spend at least six months in early access. If you really loved Othercide, I don't think there's anything here that will hugely disappoint you, just yet. You can read more about the game on Steam. Belated clarification: you do not have to be Napoleon or any other celebrated general to have opinions about Ex Sanguis. I'm not sure how Napoleon found his way into my intro, honestly.

items.title: Skyrim’s official IKEA crossover mod might be the most deftly-assembled Elder Scrolls gag ever, if not an ad blueprint other corps should follow
items.author: Mark Warren
items.summary: I didn’t think, when I saw the other day that Swedish furniture sellers IKEA had commissioned a group of modders to stick an advert for their wares in Skyrim
items.text:
I didn’t think, when I saw the other day that Swedish furniture sellers IKEA had commissioned a group of modders to stick an advert for their wares in Skyrim as an official Bethesda-approved Creation, that I’d now be sitting here noting that I dug said creation’s dungeon designs.

I am, though, because I think that sums up the entire experience of playing through Kallax Storageborn. If all you do is read a headline about it or scan through the premise with a smirk, you might assume it’s just a soulless corporate stunt aiming to play off The Elder Scrolls 5’s well-established viral memeality, but without any depth that makes it worth dedicating the time to check out. That was largely how I felt about it too, up until I learned that highly skilled Fallout 4 Sim Settlements makers Kinggath Creations were the modders behind the free creation, and decided to check their work out for myself.

The secondary motivation I had for doing so was that in-game advertising feels like it’s being floated more often than ever at the moment as a way games might help pay for themselves, as the squeeze is felt across an industry desperate for maximum financial returns. Fantasy RPGs like Skyrim are arguably among the toughest places to naturally fit such ads, especially compared to the likes of sports games or James Bond adventures with special watches.

In terms of how it fits in Tamriel, you’ll probably be glad to learn that outside of loosely meshing with Skyrim’s established mechanics, Kallax Storageborn isn’t trying too hard to pretend that its additions are in any way lore-friendly. The first time you’re overencumbered after grabbing the mod, your character is sent a magical talking telegram informing them that a solution to their storage woes can be found in a dungeon called Storereach. Yep, that’s the tone set then.

Storereach starts off as a regular Skyrim cave, but grows into a well-made Dwarven dungeon assembled mostly from recognisable vanilla building blocks. Things really kick into gear when you reach the second level, Storereach Workshop. Here, the standard swells of Skyrim’s orchestral soundtrack morph into the quiet, but unmistakable jingle of distant elevator music as you wander into a Dwarven department store. In case you’re unsure, an apparition materialises to welcome you. If you’re anything like me, you’re completely distracted by the fact that next to him are specially made Dwarven versions of IKEA’s flatbed shopping trollies.

From there, you negotiate a maze of dioramas showing off Dwarven furnishings for different rooms, some of which have buttons you can press to trigger a short demonstration by ghostly salespeople. You learn about Stenrygg seats, Tavan rugs, and Gruskok kitchen sets. The place isn’t just an empty show hall, though: there’s some unique gear and a couple of secrets that are easily missed if you don’t peek around as many corners as you might in a standard dungeon delve. While some of the gags - such as a shield with a deflection enchantment dubbed the ‘Shield of the Returns Policy’ - are rather groan-worthy, a couple properly tickled me. For instance, I stumbled across a skeleton in the loos, bearing a note indicating they’d died after simply getting lost among the labyrinthine halls of the shop. That’s the sort of joke people make about going to IKEA, rather than one the retailers themselves would necessarily make, since it suggests their signage is a bit crap. It’s the sort of touch that stops the creation feeling too reverent or robotic in its efforts to convince you to buy a flat-pack bookcase called Billy, even when it’s giving you a spell that fires the retailer’s famous Swedish meatballs.

The mod’s main draw and namesake awaits in a chamber behind the store. Armed with a tome perfectly mimicking an IKEA instruction manual, and a staff shaped like an allen key, you assemble Kallax. Once its shelves have been inserted, this unit springs to life and starts speaking in comedian Matt Berry’s dulcet tones. He’s a new follower who’ll scrape along the ground behind you as you adventure and carry all of your burdens, much like a certain base game lady whose name rhymes with an STD. Cool. This is about where I expected the adventure to end, once I’d taken one more wander around Storereach to make sure I’d maxed out a loot haul that’s very potent if you rock up at a low level fresh out of Helgen. I can confirm that because I had to start over to try the IKEA mod, as a result of still not having gotten around to making sure my mod load order’s been updated to match last month’s new patch.

Alas, my adventure with Kallax was only beginning. After I’d crafted him his own version of Skyrim’s iconic iron helmet, he had me off to two more dungeons in search first of heirlooms from his missing master, and then in search of an assistant who might be able to shed light on his reason for existence. Along the way, I grew to love not so much Berry’s array of unique lines responding to places I visited and hijinks I got up to, but the more subtly hilarious touch of his footsteps constantly resembling the low rumble of wooden furniture being dragged along stone roads and through grassy undergrowth.

Eventually, we cornered the assistant in an ancient Nordic ruin chock full of clutter that you can order Kallax to clean up in order to unblock passages. I won’t spoil the ending, but I will note that the final chamber’s utterly majestic, and that along the way you’ll encounter the last few long-running Skyrim jokes the mod’s yet to hit. Many who’re sick of such gags and have low tolerance for any form of advertising will understandably roll their eyes so many times they end up unable to stop looking at the inside of their own heads.

I found it creative, well-crafted, and self-aware enough not to grate on me. I’m not even much of a Matt Berry fan either, which I think speaks to the job Kinggath and co have done of taking what could have been a licence to phone it in and trying just as hard as they would with a non-ad project. Even if they did miss out one key item from their Dwemer emporium. Without having to lean on the mad Daedric prince Sheogorath - the ever-present crutch of any Elder Scrolls wackiness which threatens to tap on the fourth wall - they’ve created an officially rubber-stamped gag that’s worth more than five minutes of a player’s time.

That said, I don’t think Kallax Storageborn should necessarily serve as an example any corps or developers should look at when trying to insert their own palatable ads into Skyrim or any other game. The line it walks between endearing - if nakedly corporate - charm and off-putting cringe is very thin, and successfully negotiating it relies heavily on the unique blend of British and Scandinavian humour at play. If it were, say, an advert for a more American brand like Monster Energy or Little Caesars, I think it’d feel a lot more in-your-face and forced. Due to its meme-filled reputation, in large part built on the back of unofficial joke mods, Skyrim also suits this sort of tongue-in-cheek salespersonship a lot more easily than other RPGs. It’s an exception to the rule, rather than an ideal test case.

So, leave the neatly stored memories of captivating, if not overly lengthy, dungeons alone please. This shelving unit came together well, but it shouldn’t inspire legions to believe they can assemble an entire floor’s worth of bookcases without ending up with at least one screw out of place.

You learn about Stenrygg seats, Tavan rugs, and Gruskok kitchen sets. The place isn’t just an empty show hall, though: there’s some unique gear and a couple of secrets that are easily missed if you don’t peek around as many corners as you might in a standard dungeon delve. While some of the gags - such as a shield with a deflection enchantment dubbed the ‘Shield of the Returns Policy’ - are rather groan-worthy, a couple properly tickled me. For instance, I stumbled across a skeleton in the loos, bearing a note indicating they’d died after simply getting lost among the labyrinthine halls of the shop. That’s the sort of joke people make about going to IKEA, rather than one the retailers themselves would necessarily make, since it suggests their signage is a bit crap. It’s the sort of touch that stops the creation feeling too reverent or robotic in its efforts to convince you to buy a flat-pack bookcase called Billy, even when it’s giving you a spell that fires the retailer’s famous Swedish meatballs.

The mod’s main draw and namesake awaits in a chamber behind the store. Armed with a tome perfectly mimicking an IKEA instruction manual, and a staff shaped like an allen key, you assemble Kallax. Once its shelves have been inserted, this unit springs to life and starts speaking in comedian Matt Berry’s dulcet tones. He’s a new follower who’ll scrape along the ground behind you as you adventure and carry all of your burdens, much like a certain base game lady whose name rhymes with an STD. Cool. This is about where I expected the adventure to end, once I’d taken one more wander around Storereach to make sure I’d maxed out a loot haul that’s very potent if you rock up at a low level fresh out of Helgen. I can confirm that because I had to start over to try the IKEA mod, as a result of still not having gotten around to making sure my mod load order’s been updated to match last month’s new patch.

Alas, my adventure with Kallax was only beginning. After I’d crafted him his own version of Skyrim’s iconic iron helmet, he had me off to two more dungeons in search first of heirlooms from his missing master, and then in search of an assistant who might be able to shed light on his reason for existence. Along the way, I grew to love not so much Berry’s array of unique lines responding to places I visited and hijinks I got up to, but the more subtly hilarious touch of his footsteps constantly resembling the low rumble of wooden furniture being dragged along stone roads and through grassy undergrowth.

Eventually, we cornered the assistant in an ancient Nordic ruin chock full of clutter that you can order Kallax to clean up in order to unblock passages. I won’t spoil the ending, but I will note that the final chamber’s utterly majestic, and that along the way you’ll encounter the last few long-running Skyrim jokes the mod’s yet to hit. Many who’re sick of such gags and have low tolerance for any form of advertising will understandably roll their eyes so many times they end up unable to stop looking at the inside of their own heads.

I found it creative, well-crafted, and self-aware enough not to grate on me. I’m not even much of a Matt Berry fan either, which I think speaks to the job Kinggath and co have done of taking what could have been a licence to phone it in and trying just as hard as they would with a non-ad project. Even if they did miss out one key item from their Dwemer emporium. Without having to lean on the mad Daedric prince Sheogorath - the ever-present crutch of any Elder Scrolls wackiness which threatens to tap on the fourth wall - they’ve created an officially rubber-stamped gag that’s worth more than five minutes of a player’s time.

That said, I don’t think Kallax Storageborn should necessarily serve as an example any corps or developers should look at when trying to insert their own palatable ads into Skyrim or any other game. The line it walks between endearing - if nakedly corporate - charm and off-putting cringe is very thin, and successfully negotiating it relies heavily on the unique blend of British and Scandinavian humour at play. If it were, say, an advert for a more American brand like Monster Energy or Little Caesars, I think it’d feel a lot more in-your-face and forced. Due to its meme-filled reputation, in large part built on the back of unofficial joke mods, Skyrim also suits this sort of tongue-in-cheek salespersonship a lot more easily than other RPGs. It’s an exception to the rule, rather than an ideal test case.

So, leave the neatly stored memories of captivating, if not overly lengthy, dungeons alone please. This shelving unit came together well, but it shouldn’t inspire legions to believe they can assemble an entire floor’s worth of bookcases without ending up with at least one screw out of place.

items.title: “Marvel’s Wolverine” is a Bloody Good Time, Bub
items.author: Brian Tallerico
items.summary: Superheroes really are back in 2026. As if they ever left. The record-breaking success of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” segues nicely into next week’s
items.text:
Superheroes really are back in 2026. As if they ever left. The record-breaking success of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” segues nicely into next week’s long-awaited release of Insomniac’s “Marvel’s Wolverine,” a game with structural echoes of the company’s beloved “Spider-Man” games, with significantly less kid-friendly violence and more linear, intense storytelling. After a prologue/tutorial that feels a bit rocky in storytelling and gameplay, “Wolverine” settles in spectacularly, strapping players into a rollercoaster narrative and telling them not to panic. With remarkably fluid combat, gorgeous graphics, strong voice work, and compelling storytelling, this is one of the best games of 2026, which has already been a remarkably great year for gaming before roughly a dozen more intriguing titles come out before Thanksgiving. The Sony disc drama aside, it’s a good time to be a gamer.

“Marvel’s Wolverine” also owes a wonderful amount to the movies most readers have probably seen about the man with Adamantium bones. At first, it feels like it’s intentionally echoing the excellent “Logan,” the best film about this beloved character, in its sketch of a slightly older Wolverine forced into a protective role for more vulnerable mutants when the evil Bolivar Trask starts kidnapping them. The plan to eradicate mutantkind sends Logan back to his allies at Team X, including founder Nathaniel Essex and familiar faces like Sabretooth, Mystique, and Jean Grey, sketched very differently here than the Sadie Sink version from “BND.” More on that later.

After Team X rescues a group of mutants from Trask’s captivity, including Callisto, “Marvel’s Wolverine” pivots again to incorporate other comic book and film source material. It’s the kind of story that never directly mimics something you’ve seen before, but one can definitely feel the influence of Bryan Singer’s films on Logan’s search for identity and even Jean Grey’s ultimate arc (don’t worry, comic fans—I didn’t just spoil that it goes full Dark Phoenix à la the horrendous “The Last Stand”). As the story moves to Japan, it also brings in some of that country’s influence on this character, as seen cinematically in James Mangold’s underrated “The Wolverine.” You’ll even get to slice and dice your way through hundreds of members of The Hand, also seen in the best action sequence in “Brand New Day.”

And I do mean slice and dice. Parents should be warned that this game is far more violent than they may expect from the developers of “Miles Morales.” The developers don’t dull Logan’s blades in the slightest, allowing you to use them to stab, mutilate, and decapitate on a regular basis. The combat gameplay is familiar in its mix of strike, parry, dodge, and special powers, but it’s as fluid as any game like this that’s ever been released. As techniques, unlike new skills that recharge over time and one improves at the base mechanics, Wolverine becomes almost a Tasmanian Devil of a killing machine, taking enemies out at a rate befitting one of comicdom’s most beloved heroes. It gets to the point where one sees a dozen enemies and doesn’t question how to get through them but wonders why there aren’t more. By the time I got into my New Game Plus playthrough, I had fully mastered the combat of “Wolverine” as much as any game in years, and the adrenaline rush of a perfectly executed move simply never abates. I’ll honestly miss it.

Of course, a game can’t just be about decapitating fools who underestimated a man with claws. As for the rest of the experience, the set pieces are so spectacular that you can forgive the lackluster exploration. As for the latter, Logan often has to find something in a room to push the story forward, which basically just amounts to looking for the white dot that cues you to hit triangle. It’s not exactly thrilling. On the other hand, there are a couple of motorcycle set pieces that are so spectacular that you’ll wish there were more of them, and the big action sequences are as impressive as any MCU movie. The truth is that “Marvel’s Wolverine” gets the big and basic things right; so the minor connective tissue like running around the Team X facility to find the triangle that will push the story forward isn’t really a drag as much as a little break from the intensity before it becomes numbing.

Something else that elevates “Marvel’s Wolverine” over many games of this generation is its attention to environment. As you can imagine, when Logan turns into a blade whirlwind, nothing is safe, and the designers brilliantly allow you to leave a mark, whether it’s just a blade scratch on metal or something more intense. For example, you get into a fight in an arcade in Japan, and no claw machine is safe. Most combat sequences end in the kind of environmental destruction rarely seen in games where you can still take cover behind a wooden box, and it’s the kind of detail that really elevates the overall experience. It should also be noted that this game makes use of the PS5 controller in expansive ways, whether it’s a radio signal or just the hum and buzz of action. And the load times are insanely fast. You can go from startup to combat in actual seconds.

Finally, while “Marvel’s Wolverine” is incredibly fun, it’s also narratively richer than many superhero games. Without spoiling, Logan and Jean Grey become allies not just in stopping the big bad of this game but in figuring out the details of Logan’s lost past. Like in the Singer movies and some of the comic arcs, Logan is a killing machine who doesn’t really know how he got that way, and the script here lands in a place that’s both satisfying and poignant. It’s as rich as the great Uncanny X-Men arcs that this comic book fan grew up loving, and a reminder of how both superhero fiction and gaming can be so much more satisfying when it’s developed with true love, care, and mutilations.

Sony provided a review copy of this game. It is available on September 15, exclusively on PlayStation.

items.title: Bargain with demons and boat with the dead in joyful RPG heist quest anthology Thousand Hells
items.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
items.summary: You'd expect a game called Thousand Hells: The Underworld Heists to be on the depressing side, but this choose-your-own-adventure RPG anthology from the
items.text:
You'd expect a game called Thousand Hells: The Underworld Heists to be on the depressing side, but this choose-your-own-adventure RPG anthology from the designers of King of Dragon Pass is an absolute tonic. It's a witty procession of Orphic descents, in which you assemble a crew of four garrulous weirdos and pitch them against quest scenarios that might involve talking trees, holy riddlers, and conduits of boiling blood.

There's an infectious, venturesome lightness to the game, which somehow persists alongside dire blunders and supernatural calamities that may see members of your party being cursed, punctured or unhinged. I've only completed a couple of the 10 heists across two hours of play, which makes me reluctant to call this an official review, but it's got my provisional recommendation. Come, reader - get thee to Pandemonium apace.

Watch on YouTube

Thousand Hells doesn't harbour a thousand distinct hells; its variety comes, instead, from choice of party members and the canny reshuffling of story beats, which play out against handsome paintings of monoliths, bazaars, shorelines and catacombs. Each run starts with your character accepting One Last Job from some dubious power-broker in the "Byzantine-flavored" Eternal City. Perhaps you'll be looking into the untimely deaths of some princelings, or maybe you'll be escorting a murderer: either way, you'll need to trek down to an underworld that borrows ideas from Ancient Greece and Mesopotamia.

The opening interview also defines your character, as you pick from backgrounds, strengths and faults. Ho thar! I am Caroline, seasoned sailor and scout, with the bestest biceps this side of the Hungry Sea. My major shortcoming: I like to make jokes about gods.

Having created yourself, you then recruit a crew of similarly imperfect adventurers, spending Question points to decide how much you know about them to begin with. A big hand for Sethre: diplomat, pickpocket and shaman, dream-dogged and impulsive. A round of applause for Hemze: catfooted spymaster, who looks like a bull's derriere. The characters you choose will form loose relationships, reacting to each other's traits as the yarn wears on. These relationships are strongly shaped by the task at hand, which might see you keeping secrets from your colleagues, or deciding in advance that somebody ain't coming back from the Great Below.

The heist itself consists of a series of round-based encounters drawn from a pack of over 280, each with a mix of solutions depending on your party's skillset. In a pleasing tactile device that makes me think yet again of Ursula K Le Guin, encounters are resolved using bags of tokens. Each round, you pull up to four tokens from three bags. You get one bag for the character you've selected to take charge of the encounter (which means you'll be able to play more of their tokens), and one for the rest of the group. A third bag houses tide-turning boons and knowledge you may have acquired by, say, befriending a sorrowful spirit, or jailbreaking a god.

The tokens mostly reflect each character's traits, both helpful and hindersome – "Nerinai is knowledgeable", "Chisu is greedy", "Sethre has a troubled past", "Esanth knows lockpicking". You apply these tokens to one of three actions, corresponding to the scenario. You're navigating the rapids of Styx: do you focus on the rocks, or on the unruly dead crowding the stern? You're helping the Fates weave your very own destiny: do you throw the shuttle, or offer to cut the warp threads?

Other, more generic tokens might grant you resources and buffs, or rid you of debuffs. Show Some Swagger will improve a character's morale, if played successfully, while Get The Measure earns you Insight points, which let you visualise the odds of each token being successful. Any tokens and actions not used up in a round carry over to the next, so you might want to reserve any tokens that could fit several possible actions. Conversely, you'll need to figure out when to dispose of tokens that seem bound to fail. "Hemze is ugly" probably does have a use at some stage – I dunno, maybe Narcissus is working a guard post somewhere, and you can invite him to give Hemze a makeover? - but I'm not sure it's going to help me rescue some drowning merchants.

You need to win a certain number of rounds, and avoid a certain number of losses, but fumbling the encounter doesn't end the game: you might incur an injury or receive a mood penalty, perhaps even lose a character, but you'll often achieve the story objective (like crossing a river) regardless. I've rarely felt the urge to reload a save, which isn't possible anyway.

While never a taut exercise in resource juggling, the encounter design does oblige a bit of strategy, thanks to some underlying combos and questions of timing. Some actions are best performed early, boosting your chances of doing something else – disarming traps before lunging for a treasure, for instance. Some are easier to do when you're ahead or behind on victory points. A few need to be reserved for the encounter's finale.

Sometimes you get a bunch of tokens that don't entirely fit any action, and must guess how the writers will play out the implications. So far, I've found those stabs in the dark more entertaining than jarring, but there have been a couple of moments when the storycraft felt somewhat meaningless, next to the invisible tallying of points. Over the course of the heist, you also need to think about gathering items that serve as quickfix solutions, sometimes allowing you to avoid an encounter.

As you'd expect from the whole "repeatedly going to hell" premise, the encounters can be pretty macabre. During my first run, I had to deal with some hags who can shave away character traits with a nasty look. During my second, I tackled a scenario for which a positive outcome would see a character being hung from a meathook.

There are plague crows, blade tsunamis, and mesmerising demons. Worst of all, there's a poetry contest. (I won the poetry contest, mostly by alternating between mockery of my opponent and flattery of the audience.) As grim as things may get, however, the writing remains brisk and buoyant, with characters squabbling a bit and maybe revealing something about themselves when they strike out, keeping up the momentum of the tale. I've come to love these little setbacks. It's like Scheherazade turning every tumble into a cliffhanger, with her head on the line. It's the kind of game in which a clean sweep feels like a loss, because you've bleached away the reversals and pratfalls that any thrilling adventure should involve.

Thousand Hells: The Underworld Heists is out now on Steam. I reckon you should give 'er a go, especially if you enjoyed the art and writing of King of Dragon Pass and its spiritual successor, Six Ages, but found the village management element tedious. I should mention that the game's writers include Holly Nielsen, who has done stuff for RPS in the past.

A Finnish Metal Detectorist Was Shocked to Unearth a Trove of Viking Age Silver in His Hometown. Then His Detector Went Off Again

Weighing a combined ten
items.text:
A Finnish Metal Detectorist Was Shocked to Unearth a Trove of Viking Age Silver in His Hometown. Then His Detector Went Off Again

Weighing a combined ten pounds, the artifacts are estimated to be 1,000 years old and constitute Finland’s largest coin hoard of the era

A metal detectorist in southern Finland has unearthed the country’s largest hoard of Late Iron Age silver coins to date. Buried in the 11th century in what’s now the town of Sysmä, the ten-pound collection contains remnants of jewelry and likely thousands of coins.

The detectorist, Kalle Lappinen, was scanning ground in his hometown last week when his metal detector signaled. He began digging, and then his handheld probe “roared,” Lappinen tells the New York Times’ Ephrat Livni.

“With the fury of a monkey, I dug through the soil, bottom moraine and cobblestones,” he recalls. He found “a pile of coins” about 18 inches down and, once he had “recovered from the adrenaline rush,” reported it to authorities. Then, not far away, Lappinen’s metal detector signaled again, prompting him to dig a second hole—and find yet another trove of coins.

Did you know? The Staffordshire Hoard

One of the most famous discoveries by a metal detectorist was made in 2009, when Terry Herbert unearthed an astonishing

cache of some 3,500 pieces of early medieval gold and silver metalwork in Staffordshire, England, that were eventually valued at more than $5 million.

The next day, Esko Tikkala, an archaeologist at the nearby Lahti City Museums, arrived to inspect and excavate the artifacts. According to a statement from the museums, the collection includes a fragment of hacksilver, a silver bracelet, a silver charm, a silver bead and many silver coins—which have not yet been cleaned, separated or counted. The coins alone weigh just under ten pounds; experts say there must be thousands.

“There are quite a lot of coins in this hoard,” and they await detailed analysis, Tikkala tells Live Science’s Tom Metcalfe. “There will definitely be scientific articles published on the hoard as a whole, as well as more detailed studies of the coins themselves.”

The hoard likely dates to between about 1000 and 1050 C.E., Tikkala says. This half-century corresponds with the tail end of the Viking Age, which historians typically confine to about 793 C.E.—when Vikings raided Lindisfarne in Britain—through 1066, the date of the Norman Conquest. Lahti City Museums have thus classified the hoard as a “Viking Age” find.

“The term ‘Viking Age’ does not imply that there were Vikings in Finland,” Tikkala explains. “We have no sources suggesting that Finland was ‘Viking’ in the same sense as regions of present-day Sweden, Norway and Denmark.”

Though Finland isn’t Scandinavian and wasn’t Viking territory, by the 11th century, some Swedes had settled on its southern coasts. As Toni Paukku, an archaeologist at the Lahti Museums, tells the Times, “Finland was strongly connected to the Scandinavian cultural sphere, boosted by the trade of Scandinavian seafarers—some of whom were indeed Vikings—across the Baltic Sea.”

The silver hoard found by Lappinen was buried in two birch-bark containers, about 40 feet apart, per the statement. Experts don’t know why it was buried, but historians do know that the close of the Viking Age was an unstable period in Finland, as Swedes and Danes raided its regions where Finns, Russians and Germans traded.

“Intentionally hidden treasures like these are somewhat common for this era in Finland,” Paukku tells the Times, citing societal unrest due to external threats. “One can only say that whoever they”—the people who hid the silver—“were, they did not come back to collect the treasure. … No burials appear to be associated with the hoard.”

Lappinen’s find marks the latest in a remarkable tally of silver discoveries this year. Just over a week ago, a Dane landscaping in his backyard accidentally unearthed Denmark’s largest hoard of Viking silver, and in April, metal detectorists in Norway found their country’s largest deposit of Viking silver. It shows that “detectorists can produce a considerable amount of new valuable information about the past, not the least because they (as in this case) search in areas that professional archaeologists do not go to.”

items.text:
Did You Suffer a Sweltering August? You Weren’t Alone. It Tied for the Month With the Hottest Global Temperatures on Record

Last month, the air temperature averaged 62.53 degrees Fahrenheit, tying with July 2023 as the toastiest month ever documented by the European Union’s climate service

Sara Hashemi
| Daily Correspondent

September 11, 2026 12:57 p.m.

If you thought this August was especially hot, you aren’t wrong. According to the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service, last month tied with July 2023 as the hottest month on its record, which dates back to 1940.

The global surface air temperature averaged 62.53 degrees Fahrenheit in August. That’s almost 3 degrees above pre-industrial levels, which exceeds the 2.7-degree threshold set by the Paris Agreement, an international treaty on climate change adopted by nearly 200 nations in 2015.

“These observations show how climate change is driving extremes across both the atmosphere and the oceans,” says Samantha Burgess, a climate scientist and deputy director of Copernicus, in the statement. “The impacts of these conditions are increasingly being felt by communities, economies and ecosystems across the world.”

Western Europe had its hottest summer ever as it dealt with back-to-back heatwaves that led to at least 35,000 deaths. So did the contiguous United States, where the average temperature in August hit 75.6 degrees—3.5 degrees above the 20th-century average. It was the warmest season on the U.S.’s record, which stretches back to 1895, according to the National Centers for Environmental Information. July was even hotter, averaging 76.9 degrees and breaking the infamous Dust Bowl record set in July 1936, per Jeff Masters and Bob Henson at Yale Climate Connections.

Other parts of the world were also drier than average, including northern Mexico, parts of Canada, the Maghreb, part of the Horn of Africa, Siberia and large parts of Asia, China, South America, South Africa and northern Australia, according to Copernicus. And at 69.9 degrees, the average sea surface temperature outside the polar regions was the highest on record for any August, passing the record previously set for the month in 2023.

According to Copernicus, the record-breaking summer heat likely arose from two factors: a strengthening El Niño in the Pacific Ocean and global heating from human use of fossil fuels. Scientists note that the naturally occurring climate pattern of El Niño alone is not responsible for these temperatures.

“While El Niño is starting to ramp up the heat, the underlying driver remains our relentless burning of fossil fuels. Climate change makes every El Niño hotter, and until we stop burning coal, oil and gas these record-shattering months will simply keep on coming,” says Friederike Otto, a climate scientist at Imperial College London, to Seth Borenstein at the Associated Press.

Quick fact: El Niño events have been growing stronger

Using records captured in corals, a study published in August found that although El Niño climate swings occur naturally, they’ve become stronger in recent decades. That’s probably happening because humans have been heating up the planet.

The Copernicus finding follows a United Nations report that warned that passing the Paris Agreement’s 2.7-degree threshold is probably unavoidable. According to the U.N. document, titled “Limiting Overshoot” and published on September 2, the world now needs to focus on minimizing peak warming and finding ways to bring temperatures back down.

Simon Stiell, the executive secretary of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, writes on social media that the Copernicus report is “another stark warning sign from our heating planet,” and underscores the need for humans to stop burning coal, oil and gas. “This is the spiraling price of humanity’s fossil fuel addiction, and the global climate crisis it is fueling.”

Clair Barnes, an extreme weather researcher at Imperial College London, echoes that sentiment. “Until we stop burning fossil fuels, these records will continue to tumble, and the extremes will worsen faster than we are able to adapt,” she tells Matt McGrath at the BBC News. “Crucially, how much worse we allow it to get remains within our hands.”

items.text:
Designers and Computer Scientists Create New Decoy Fonts That Humans Can Read but A.I. Bots Cannot

To prevent the trawling and theft of human writing, font-makers are employing both old and new illusions to outsmart large language models

As the deployment of A.I. tools into search engines, text messaging and writing platforms becomes increasingly conspicuous and pervasive, some researchers are seeking new ways to insulate words written by humans from the reach of trawling bots and A.I. agents.

The camouflaging technique is a modern-day version of an optical illusion known as hybrid imaging, which was made famous in 2007 when researchers at MIT created a portrait in which both Marilyn Monroe and Albert Einstein were identifiable, depending on the distance of the viewer.

Whereas those images were created to better understand human perception, Decoy Font was inspired by a desire for privacy. The font features two layers of text: one foregrounded in clear outlines and a second dark and blurred in the background. It offers human writers the chance to create cheeky juxtapositional messages, hiding the blurred “Happy Human,” for example, behind a crisp “Sorry Robot.”

MixFont’s first attempt at an anti-A.I. typeface was called Ghost Font: a slightly dizzying display that placed moving words atop a television-static-like background that also constantly shifted. The company acknowledged that it wasn’t a traditional font, because the message was readable only in a video format, but the design successfully demonstrated the limits of A.I. perception.

“I was inspired to make Ghost Font one day after texting with my mom, and I noticed that A.I. kept trying to summarize our messages, many times incorrectly,” Eric Lu, MixFont’s founder, tells Forbes’ Leslie Katz. “I was annoyed that it was being so intrusive in our private conversation, and I started brainstorming ways that I could potentially communicate without A.I. reading everything.”

Other designers have also experimented in recent months with tricking A.I. trawlers.

Fun fact: The first font

The father of the printing press, Johann Gutenberg, is largely credited with having created the first Western typeface.

His black-letter font was designed to mimic the handwritten calligraphy of monks.

In July, a collaboration of studios including Seneda & Abrucio and PlayType released ShieldFont, a typeface that scrambles text for automated scrapers. The font replaces roughly half of all “content words”—nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs—with random other words in its source code, such that the writing taken by bots is nonsensical. More than 90 percent of the resultant gibberish is rejected by quality filters, Fast Company’s Hunter Schwarz reports.

“A sentence is a sequence of decisions,” ShieldFont’s creators write in their white paper, explaining that a primary motivator for their work was to block the theft of human writing by A.I. models. “When I write, I am choosing this word rather than that one, putting this clause before that one, deciding what to leave out. The finished paragraph is a record of thinking that took effort to do. ... We are being asked to hand over the work, and to train our own replacement with it, and to do both without being told.”

ShieldFont: A Typeface that Poisons Unauthorized AI Training

MixFont “started as an exploration of how A.I. and typography intersect, but it was also meant to raise awareness of the growing reach and capabilities of A.I.,” Lu tells Dezeen’s Rima Sabina Aouf. “I think the reaction to the font shows that there are many folks who feel strong A.I. fatigue and want a way to defend themselves against the presence of A.I. in their lives.”
